slides.title: Introduction to Probability
bullets: A first introduction to probability for science and engineering students
Topics: sample spaces and events, axioms of probability
Conditional probability, independence and Bayes' theorem
Discrete random variables, expectation and variance
Each chapter ends with a short worked example

slides.title: Random Experiments and Sample Spaces
bullets: Random experiment: outcome cannot be predicted with certainty (e.g. coin toss, bulb lifetime)
Sample space S: set of all possible outcomes
One die roll: S = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}
Event: a subset of the sample space, e.g. "roll is even" A = {2, 4, 6}
An event occurs when the outcome belongs to it; empty set is impossible, S is certain
slides.notes: Emphasize that events are sets of outcomes.

slides.title: Combining Events
bullets: Union of A and B: A or B occurs
Intersection of A and B: both occur
Complement of A: A does not occur
Mutually exclusive (disjoint): cannot occur together, intersection is empty
Example: A = even, B = greater than 3; union {2, 4, 5, 6}, intersection {4, 6}
slides.notes: Worked example from the die roll.

slides.title: Kolmogorov's Axioms
bullets: A probability measure assigns a number P(A) to every event A
Probabilities are never negative
The probability of the whole sample space is one
Probability of a union of mutually exclusive events is the sum of their probabilities

equations.explanation: Every event has non-negative probability, and the certain event has probability one.

equations.latex: P ( A \cup B ) = P ( A ) + P ( B ) \text { if } A \cap B = \emptyset
equations.explanation: For disjoint events, the probability that one or the other occurs is the sum of their probabilities.

slides.notes: These three axioms are the foundation for all later rules.

slides.title: Consequences of the Axioms
bullets: Complement of A has probability one minus P(A)
The impossible event has probability zero
Addition rule for any two events subtracts the intersection, which would be counted twice
Equally likely outcomes: P(event) = outcomes in event / total outcomes
Fair die: P(even) = 3/6 = 1/2

equations.latex: P ( A \cup B ) = P ( A ) + P ( B ) - P ( A \cap B )
equations.explanation: General addition rule: add the probabilities and remove the double-counted overlap.

slides.notes: The addition rule holds for events that are not necessarily disjoint.

slides.title: Conditional Probability
bullets: Describes how probability of an event changes when another event is known to have occurred
P(A given B) is defined when P(B) is greater than zero
Multiplication rule: P(A and B) = P(A given B) times P(B)

equations.latex: P ( A \, | \, B ) = \frac { P ( A \cap B ) } { P ( B ) }
equations.explanation: The probability of A given B is the probability of both occurring divided by the probability of B.

equations.latex: P ( A \cap B ) = P ( A \, | \, B ) P ( B )
equations.explanation: Multiplication rule, obtained by rearranging the definition of conditional probability.

slides.notes: Multiplication rule follows directly from the definition.

slides.title: Total Probability and Independence
bullets: Law of total probability splits P(A) over a partition into disjoint cases B1, ..., Bn
Independent: knowing one occurred does not change the probability of the other
Equivalently, P of the intersection is the product of the probabilities
Independence is not mutual exclusivity: disjoint events with positive probabilities are always dependent

equations.explanation: The probability of A is a weighted sum of its conditional probabilities over all cases of a partition.

equations.latex: P ( A \cap B ) = P ( A ) P ( B )
equations.explanation: Condition for A and B to be independent.

slides.notes: Stress the common confusion between independent and disjoint events.

slides.title: Worked Example: Two Aces
bullets: Draw two cards from a deck without replacement
P(both aces) = 4/52 times 3/51, about 0.0045
The second factor is a conditional probability: the first ace has been removed

slides.title: Bayes' Theorem
bullets: Reverses a conditional probability
Expresses P(B given A) using P(A given B), which is often easier to know
P(B) is the prior probability; P(B given A) is the posterior probability
Denominator P(A) is usually computed with the law of total probability

equations.latex: P ( B \ | \ A ) = \frac { P ( A \ | \ B ) P ( B ) } { P ( A ) }
equations.explanation: The posterior probability of B given A equals the likelihood of A given B times the prior of B, divided by P(A).

slides.notes: Connect the denominator to the law of total probability from the previous section.

slides.title: Worked Example: Medical Test
bullets: Disease affects 1% of the population
Test detects 99% of sick people; 5% false positives among healthy people
The prior is so small that most positive results are false positives
slides.notes: A classic illustration of the importance of the prior.

slides.title: Random Variables, Mean and Variance
bullets: Random variable: function assigning a number to each outcome
Discrete: takes a finite or countable number of values
PMF p(x): probability the variable equals x; non-negative and sums to one
Expectation: probability-weighted average; variance: spread around the mean

equations.latex: E [ X ] = \sum _ { x } x \, p ( x )
equations.explanation: The mean is the sum of each value weighted by its probability.
The variance is the mean of the square minus the square of the mean.

slides.title: Linearity and Fair Die Example
bullets: Expectation is linear: E[aX + b] = a E[X] + b for any constants a, b
Var(aX + b) = a squared times Var(X): adding a constant does not change the spread
E[X squared] = 91/6, so variance = 91/6 - 12.25, about 2.92

equations.latex: E [ a X + b ] = a E [ X ] + b
equations.explanation: Scaling and shifting a random variable scales and shifts its mean in the same way.

equations.latex: Var ( a X + b ) = a ^ { 2 } Var ( X )
equations.explanation: Scaling multiplies the variance by the square of the factor; shifting has no effect.
